prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a logical memory experiment on a distance-3 rotated surface-code patch (3 rounds, Z-basis readout), under uniform depolarizing circuit noise with p = 0.003. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
For the FTPrimitiveBench logical-memory primitive

* primitive = memory
* patch = rotated surface code, distance $d_X=d_Z=3$
* syndrome rounds $t=3$ with Z-basis initialization / measurement
* noise = uniform depolarizing circuit-level, $p=0.003$
* decoder = PyMatching, shots = 20 000, seed = 42

The FTPrimitiveBench memory experiment is the baseline primitive for characterising how a surface-code patch preserves an encoded state across repeated syndrome-extraction rounds: a logical eigenstate is initialized, protected for $t$ rounds, and measured in the same basis. [^9]

Noise-model description used by FTPrimitiveBench:

The baseline assigns the same $p$ to SPAM, gate error and idling errors. A structured noise model is from one of the three hardware-motivated families: Pauli $Z$-biased noise …; measurement-biased noise …; and non-uniform depolarizing noise … [^6]

FTPrimitiveBench supports both custom specifications and representative structured noise families, including Pauli-noise bias, measurement-biased noise, and spatial or spatio-temporal non-uniformity, together with generators for a core set of surface-code Clifford primitives: logical memory, lattice surgery, logical Hadamard via transversal gate, and the logical phase (S) gate via lattice surgery. [^5]

The current implementation supports four foundational primitives: logical memory, the transversal Hadamard, lattice surgery, and the lattice-surgery-based phase ($S$) gate. [^9]

Simulation result

* logical error rate: $0.01475$
* 95% Wilson interval: $[0.01317,\;0.01652]$
* std. error: $0.000852$
* failures / shots: $295 / 20\,000$
* qubits / detectors / observables: $17 / 24 / 1$
* circuit SHA-256: `c3a1f01a21f3b271eae042bb4bafd40dcc183d8d89ea5f31452021a364b7560b`

The memory experiment benchmarks the ability of a logical qubit to preserve quantum information while stationary, and serves as the baseline for estimating the logical error rate (LER). [^9]

Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench memory primitive for a rotated surface-code patch under uniform circuit-level depolarizing noise

* Primitive: logical memory  
* Patch: rotated surface code, $d_X = d_Z = 5$  
* Rounds: $t = 5$ syndrome-extraction rounds  
* Logical basis: Z-basis readout, transversal init / meas  
* Noise: uniform, $p = 0.005$  – baseline assigns the same $p$ to SPAM, gate error and idling errors [^7]
* Decoder: PyMatching  – MWPM is the workhorse decoder for the surface code and other graphlike codes [^4]
* Shots: 20 000, seed 42

Result from FTPrimitiveBench arXiv:2605.04049:

* logical error rate = 0.03035
* standard error = 0.00121
* 95 % Wilson interval: [0.02806 , 0.03282]
* failures / shots: 607 / 20 000
* circuit resources: 49 qubits, 120 detectors, 1 observable
* circuit SHA-256: e80bdf42337b5f6c93deeeda17418d904bcfb3559cae8a4bef0f42f9416d9641

The surface code is a topological CSS code on a 2-D square lattice with plaquette $B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p} Z_e$ and vertex $A_v=\prod_{e\ni v} X_e$ stabilizers, encoding $k=1$ with distance $d=L$ for a planar $L\times L$ patch [^1]. Syndrome extraction is repeated over many rounds so measurement errors appear as vertical edges in the $(2+1)$-D space-time graph that MWPM decodes [^2]. The quoted threshold $\sim1\%$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise is the standard symmetric benchmark [^1][^3].

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a logical memory experiment on a rotated surface-code patch with X distance 5 and Z distance 3 (5 rounds, Z-basis readout), under Z-biased Pauli noise with p = 0.003 and bias factor 10. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench memory primitive (arXiv:2605.04049) was run for a rotated surface-code patch with the requested geometry and noise.

* Primitive: memory
* Patch: $d_X = 5$, $d_Z = 3$, $t = 5$ rounds, $\bar Z$-basis readout
* Noise: Pauli-biased, baseline $p=0.003$, bias axis $Z$, bias factor $\eta =10$

Under the FTPrimitiveBench noise family Pauli $Z$-biased noise every depolarizing channel is replaced by a homogeneous asymmetric Pauli channel with weights 
$p_X = p_Y = p/(\eta+2)$, $p_Z = \eta p/(\eta+2)$ and bias factor $\eta\ge 1$ [^5].  
The primitive generator automatically handles detector annotations and logical observable definitions and the current implementation supports logical memory, the transversal Hadamard, lattice surgery, and the lattice-surgery-based phase ($S$) gate [^7].

Simulation output, decoded with PyMatching:

* Shots: 20 000, seed 42
* Circuit SHA-256: fc1dfa367d299495dac40a8bc20f27b3da324306191d4b8e30e45ffdd4615a27
* Qubits / detectors / observables: 29 / 72 / 1
* Logical failures observed: 3

Logical error rate
* $\hat p_L = 0.00015$
* Standard error $\approx 8.66\times10^{-5}$
* 95 % Wilson interval: $[5.10\times10^{-5},\;4.41\times10^{-4}]$

The surface code is a topological CSS code on a 2D square lattice with plaquette $B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p}Z_e$ and vertex $A_v=\prod_{e\ni v}X_e$ stabilizers, encoding $k=1$ with distance $d=L$ for a planar patch [^1]. Repeated syndrome extraction is the heartbeat of QEC memory: each round produces a syndrome that a decoder turns into a correction, and under circuit-level noise decoding is performed in the $(2+1)$-D space-time graph [^2]. Minimum-weight perfect matching is the workhorse decoder for the surface code, pairing flipped detectors with Edmonds’ blossom and edge weights $-\log p_e$ [^3].

answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench memory primitive for the rotated surface code

* Primitive: `memory` on a square rotated patch with `x_distance = z_distance = 5`
* Rounds: 5 syndrome rounds, Z-basis logical readout `meas_basis = Z`
* Noise: measurement-biased family. In FTPrimitiveBench the baseline assigns the same $p$ to SPAM, gate error and idling errors and a structured noise model is from one of three hardware-motivated families: Pauli $Z$-biased noise, *measurement-biased noise, in which only the per-measurement Pauli-flip rate is rescaled to $\eta p$—gate, reset, and idling channels held at the baseline—homogeneously across qubits and rounds with $\eta\ge 1$*; and non-uniform depolarizing noise [^5].
* Physical error rate: $p = 0.003$, measurement bias factor $\eta = 5.0$ → per-measurement Pauli-flip rate $\eta p$.
* Decoder: PyMatching, as used by FTPrimitiveBench.

Simulation result, 20 000 shots, seed 42:

* Circuit: rotated surface code memory, 49 qubits, 120 detectors, 1 observable
* Logical error rate: $0.0234$
* Standard error: $0.001069$
* 95 % Wilson interval: $[0.0214,\;0.0256]$

468 failures out of 20 000 shots.  
Circuit SHA-256: `2136f89b4030762b8af1d1bb2ee82fae2117fe79427d160010956d3ad8b42506`

FTPrimitiveBench is the systematic benchmarking approach for studying how key logical primitives interact with varying hardware-motivated noise assumptions and supports Pauli-noise bias, measurement-biased noise and spatial/spatio-temporal non-uniformity together with generators for surface-code Clifford primitives: logical memory, lattice surgery, logical Hadamard via transversal gate, and the logical phase (S) gate via lattice surgery [^4]. It unifies noise-model specification with stabilizer-circuit representations of logical computation, enabling controlled and reproducible evaluation of logical error rates across diverse noise profiles, hardware assumptions and decoding strategies [^9].

Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench memory simulation for a rotated surface-code patch

* Primitive: memory, square patch $d=5$ ($x\_distance=5$, $z\_distance=5$)
* Rounds: 5, measurement basis Z
* Noise: nonuniform with baseline $p=0.003$, relative scatter $\sigma=0.3$, seed 42
* Decoder: PyMatching

Results from the run

* Shots: 20 000
* Logical failures: 179
* Logical error rate: $0.00895$
* Std. error: $0.000666$
* 95 % Wilson interval: $[0.00774,\;0.01035]$

Circuit metadata: 49 qubits, 120 detectors, 1 observable, SHA-256 `c803967fd2b7c7e84dd8accd5fba1c7ba6f90e28cef67583dd1140726aae2bd2`.

FTPrimitiveBench unifies noise-model specification with stabilizer-circuit representations of logical computation, enabling controlled and reproducible evaluation of logical error rates across diverse noise profiles, hardware assumptions, and decoding strategies [^8]. It provides a flexible noise-model interface that decouples physical noise specification from circuit generation, accompanied by four built-in hardware-motivated families that extend beyond uniform depolarizing noise [^5]; the four families include Pauli-noise bias, measurement-biased noise, and spatial or spatio-temporal non-uniformity, together with generators for a core set of surface-code Clifford primitives: logical memory, lattice surgery, logical Hadamard via transversal gate, and the logical phase (S) gate via lattice surgery [^5].

Noise-model specification is exposed at four levels of granularity—global, per-component, per-round, and per-(component, round)—so a fully customized noise model can capture both a hardware calibration profile and the physical-overhead errors induced by compilation [^11]. Stabilizer simulation samples physical faults from the noise model and decodes detection events to estimate the probability of logical failure; this Monte Carlo approach is the standard methodology for benchmarking QEC protocols [^10].

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a transversal Hadamard on a distance-5 rotated surface-code patch: 5 rounds before and 5 rounds after one transversal H layer, Z-basis readout, under uniform depolarizing circuit noise with p = 0.003. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench transversal-H primitive on a rotated surface-code patch

* Primitive: `transversal_h` with a square rotated patch `x_distance = z_distance = 5`
* Pre-gate SE rounds `t_pre = 5`, post-gate SE rounds `t_post = 5`, one transversal Hadamard layer in the middle
* Readout: Z basis, `meas_basis = Z`
* Noise: uniform circuit-level depolarizing, `p = 0.003`
* Decoder: PyMatching
* Shots = 20 000, seed = 42

The generator described in FTPrimitiveBench builds the logical Hadamard primitive by applying physical Hadamard gates to every data qubit within the logical patch, mapping $\bar{X}\leftrightarrow\bar{Z}$ while interchanging the roles of $X$- and $Z$-type stabilizers. [^10] The spacetime volume mirrors the memory experiment: $V_{\mathrm{Had}} = d_X d_Z (t_{\mathrm{pre}}+t_{\mathrm{post}}+1)$. [^10] FTPrimitiveBench automatically handles detector annotations and logical observable definitions for the four foundational primitives: logical memory, the transversal Hadamard, lattice surgery, and the lattice-surgery-based phase $S$ gate. [^10]

Simulation result

* `num_qubits` = 49, `num_detectors` = 264, `num_observables` = 1
* `circuit_sha256` = a1bdc37dea1838de11fed52a830152afd7be5751fcb5725718230477cd90b21f
* Failures = 396 / 20 000

Logical error rate

* $\hat p_L = 0.0198$
* Standard error = 0.000985
* 95 % Wilson interval: $[0.01796,\;0.02182]$

i.e. $p_L = 0.0198 \pm 0.0010$, 95 % CI ≈ 0.018 – 0.022 per experiment under uniform depolarizing $p=0.003$ with PyMatching decoding.

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a transversal Hadamard on a distance-5 rotated surface-code patch: 5 rounds before and 5 rounds after one transversal H layer, Z-basis readout, under Z-biased Pauli noise with p = 0.003 and bias factor 10. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
Using FTPrimitiveBench the transversal-H primitive is generated for a rotated surface-code patch with a transversal Hadamard layer sandwiched by syndrome extraction. The primitive is:

* `primitive = transversal_h`
* square patch `d_X = d_Z = 5`
* `pre_rounds = 5`, `post_rounds = 5`  → spacetime volume $V_{\rm Had}=d_X d_Z (t_{\rm pre}+t_{\rm post}+1)$
* measurement basis Z, memory/measurement experiment construction as in Fig. memory-primitive
* noise = Pauli-biased with baseline $p=0.003$, bias axis Z, bias factor $\eta=10$

FTPrimitiveBench defines the structured noise families and the primitive generators:

> *sol* unifies noise-model specification with stabilizer-circuit representations of logical computation, enabling controlled and reproducible evaluation of logical error rates across diverse noise profiles, hardware assumptions, and decoding strategies. [^6]
> It provides (1) a flexible noise-model interface that decouples physical noise specification from circuit generation, accompanied by four built-in hardware-motivated families that extend beyond uniform depolarizing noise; and (2) a high-level generator for surface-code logical primitives spanning the logical Clifford group, including memory, lattice surgery, transversal Hadamard, and the lattice-surgery-based phase gate. [^6]

The transversal Hadamard primitive is constructed by applying physical Hadamard gates to every data qubit within the logical patch. This operation maps $\bar{X}\leftrightarrow\bar{Z}$ while interchanging the roles of $X$- and $Z$-type stabilizers. [^7]

The Z-biased Pauli noise model used is

* $p_X = p_Y = p/(\eta+2)$, $p_Z = \eta p/(\eta+2)$ with bias factor $\eta\ge1$,

as described for FTPrimitiveBench:

> A structured noise model is from one of the three hardware-motivated families: Pauli $Z$-biased noise, in which every depolarizing channel is replaced by a homogeneous asymmetric Pauli channel with weights $p_X{=}p_Y{=}p/(\eta{+}2)$, $p_Z{=}\eta p/(\eta{+}2)$ and bias factor $\eta\!\ge\!1$; [^9]

Detector annotations and logical observable definitions are handled automatically:

> *sol* automatically handles detector annotations and logical observable definitions. This allows for the seamless generation of Detector Error Models (DEMs) which can be passed directly to simulation and decoders pipeline. The current implementation supports four foundational primitives: logical memory, the transversal Hadamard, lattice surgery, and the lattice-surgery--based phase ($S$) gate. [^7]

Simulation with Stim and PyMatching decoding:

* circuit SHA-256: `449b3fbf342ae1bd091cdde3e0e96bb6841d6d3280936532e5a4627d4db0aa4a`
* qubits = 49, detectors = 264, observables = 1
* shots = 20 000, seed = 42, decoder = PyMatching

Result

* logical error rate = 0.0176
* standard error = 0.00093
* 95 % Wilson interval: [0.01587 , 0.01952]
* failures = 352 / 20 000

The transversal Hadamard exchanges $X$ and $Z$ channels mid-circuit and is therefore not bias-preserving:

> Asymmetric patches substantially improve logical memory and lattice surgery under $Z$-biased noise, but this advantage diminishes for the transversal Hadamard, which exchanges $X$ and $Z$ channels mid-circuit and is therefore not bias-preserving. [^10]

Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
With FTPrimitiveBench the rotated surface-code transversal Hadamard primitive was generated with:

* patch: distance $d_X = d_Z = 3$ rotated surface code, $n=17$ data+ancilla qubits
* primitive: `transversal_h`, $t_{\rm pre}=3$ syndrome-extraction rounds, one transversal $H$ layer on every data qubit, $t_{\rm post}=3$ rounds
* readout: $Z$-basis memory experiment, i.e. logical $\bar Z$ initialization and final measurement
* noise: uniform circuit-level depolarizing, $p=0.003$
* decoding: PyMatching on the Stim detector-error model
* shots = 20 000, seed = 42

Circuit metadata returned by FTPrimitiveBench:
* num detectors = 56, num observables = 1
* circuit SHA-256 = `3b99da3b338f13d2e502085143f7460ae86fe01df288028e2b1c30fb224b6ab7`
* source: FTPrimitiveBench (arXiv:2605.04049), commit b75fbd1

Logical error rate

* logical error rate = $0.0361$
* 95 % Wilson interval: $[0.0336,\;0.0388]$
* standard error $\approx 0.00132$
* failures = 722 / 20 000 shots

The surface code is a topological CSS code on a 2-D square lattice with plaquette $B_p=\prod_{e\in\partial p}Z_e$ and vertex $A_v=\prod_{e\ni v}X_e$ stabilizers, $k=1$, $d=L$ for a planar $L\times L$ patch【1†L9-L21】. A logical $\bar X$ connects two rough boundaries and a logical $\bar Z$ connects two smooth boundaries, both of weight $L$【1†L23-L25】.

Syndrome extraction measures each stabilizer generator with an ancilla and repeated rounds are required because the extraction circuit is noisy; measurement errors appear as vertical edges in the $(2+1)$-D space-time graph used by decoders【2†L22-L28】. The rotated surface code uses weight-4 interior stabilizers and weight-2 boundary stabilizers in a checkerboard pattern, with logical operators spanning the lattice between opposite boundaries【10†L1-L5】.

FTPrimitiveBench implements the transversal Hadamard primitive by applying physical Hadamard gates to every data qubit within the logical patch; this maps $\bar X\leftrightarrow\bar Z$ while interchanging the roles of $X$- and $Z$-type stabilizers. Parameters are patch distances $d_X,d_Z$ and pre-gate SE rounds $t_{\rm pre}$ and post-gate SE rounds $t_{\rm post}$; the space-time volume is $V_{\rm Had}=d_Xd_Z(t_{\rm pre}+t_{\rm post}+1)$【7†L1-L9】. The transversal Hadamard exchanges $X$ and $Z$ channels mid-circuit and is therefore not bias-preserving【11†L1-L4】.

Uniform depolarizing noise is the symmetric single-qubit channel $\mathcal E(\rho)=(1-p)\rho+\frac p3(X\rho X+Y\rho Y+Z\rho Z)$ and the two-qubit version applies one of the 15 non-identity Paulis with probability $p/15$; it is the default circuit-level benchmark for thresholds, e.g. $\sim1\%$ for the surface code【3†L9-L15】.

MWPM models decoding as minimum-weight perfect matching on the detector graph with edge weights $-\log p_e$, i.e. the most likely independent-error matching, and is the workhorse decoder for the surface code under circuit-level noise【4†L9-L16】.

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a transversal Hadamard on a rotated surface-code patch with X distance 3 and Z distance 5: 5 rounds before and 5 rounds after one transversal H layer, Z-basis readout, under Z-biased Pauli noise with p = 0.003 and bias factor 10. Use 20,000 shots and seed 42, decode with PyMatching, and report the logical error rate with its 95% interval.
answer_text:
FTPrimitiveBench simulation of the rotated surface-code transversal Hadamard primitive with the requested parameters:

* patch: rotated surface code, $d_X=3$, $d_Z=5$
* rounds: $t_{\mathrm{pre}}=5$, transversal $H_L$ layer, $t_{\mathrm{post}}=5$
* readout: Z-basis
* noise: Pauli-biased, $p=0.003$, bias axis $Z$, bias factor $\eta=10$
* decoder: PyMatching
* shots = 20 000, seed = 42

The primitive is generated as in FTPrimitiveBench, where the logical Hadamard $H_L$ is implemented transversally by applying a physical Hadamard to every data qubit within the logical patch, mapping $\bar X\leftrightarrow\bar Z$ while interchanging the roles of $X$- and $Z$-type stabilizers. The generator automatically tracks this transformation, ensuring that subsequent rounds reflect the rotated patch orientation and swapped parity checks. [^6]

The built-in hardware-motivated noise families include Pauli $Z$-biased noise, in which every depolarizing channel is replaced by a homogeneous asymmetric Pauli channel with weights $p_X{=}p_Y{=}p/(\eta{+}2)$, $p_Z{=}\eta p/(\eta{+}2)$ and bias factor $\eta\ge1$. [^10]

Simulation output:

* logical error rate = 0.0805
* 95 % Wilson interval = [0.0768 , 0.0844]
* std error = 0.00192
* failures = 1 610 / 20 000
* qubits = 29, detectors = 152, observables = 1
* circuit SHA-256 = 254121648b6f3bbbcb1ea4a772fc00416e62957502577695e120aaef1ebcfd7c

The rotated surface code is a topological CSS code on a 2-D square lattice with $k=1$ and distance $d=L$ for a planar code with rough/smooth boundaries, and logical $\bar X$ / $\bar Z$ are strings connecting rough/smooth boundaries of weight $L$. [^1]

Syndrome extraction is repeated over many rounds so that measurement errors appear as vertical edges and data errors as horizontal ones in the $(2+1)$-D space-time graph on which MWPM decodes. [^2]

Minimum-weight perfect matching models decoding as pairing flipped detectors with minimum total weight, with edge weights $-\log p_e$, and is the workhorse decoder for the surface code. [^3]

prompt: Using FTPrimitiveBench, simulate a ZZ lattice-surgery merge and split between two patches, each a distance-3 rotated surface-code patch, with bridge length 1 and 3 rounds before, during and after the merge, under uniform depolarizing circuit noise with p = 0.003. * primitive: `lattice_surgery`
* patch: square rotated surface code `x_distance = 3 , z_distance = 3`

The simulation uses the FTPrimitiveBench noise-model interface and primitive generators described in the benchmark suite. FTPrimitiveBench unifies noise-model specification with stabilizer-circuit representations of logical computation, enabling controlled and reproducible evaluation of logical error rates across diverse noise profiles, hardware assumptions, and decoding strategies. [^8]

It provides a flexible noise-model interface that decouples physical noise specification from circuit generation, accompanied by four built-in hardware-motivated families that extend beyond uniform depolarizing noise [^9]; and a high-level generator for surface-code logical primitives spanning the logical Clifford group, including memory, lattice surgery, transversal Hadamard, and the lattice-surgery-based phase $S$ gate [^8]. The current implementation supports four foundational primitives: logical memory, the transversal Hadamard, lattice surgery, and the lattice-surgery--based phase $S$ gate. [^10]

Structured noise families are applied in the same way to every supported primitive, so a noise feature studied in the context of memory can also be examined against lattice surgery or the phase gate without rewriting the circuit generator. [^7] The baseline assigns the same $p$ to SPAM, gate error and idling errors. A structured noise model is from one of the three hardware-motivated families: Pauli $Z$-biased noise, in which every depolarizing channel is replaced by a homogeneous asymmetric Pauli channel with weights $p_X{=}p_Y{=}p/(\eta{+}2)$, $p_Z{=}\eta p/(\eta{+}2)$ and bias factor $\eta\!\ge\!1$ [^11].
